meta.headline: UK inflation jumps to 3.1% as energy costs soar

relevance.reason: The article reports a change in UK inflation, explains the cause and discusses the effects, which is core Theme 2 content.

mapping.justification: The article is about the UK inflation rate, its cause in higher energy costs and how policymakers might respond.

paragraphs: The UK's annual inflation rate rose to 3.1% in August, up from 2.9% in July and the first reading above 3% since March. The result matched what economists had expected.

The Office for National Statistics said the increase was driven mainly by motor fuel, where prices were 23% higher than a year earlier. Petrol rose by 9.1 pence per litre and diesel by 14.2 pence per litre between July and August. Household energy costs, including electricity and gas, were 6% higher than a year before. Crude oil is above $100 a barrel because of the war involving Iran, and the UK is a net importer of energy, which makes it vulnerable to outside shocks.

The key question for economists is whether higher energy costs are spreading to other prices. An economist at ING pointed out that food inflation slipped to 1.1% and that inflation in energy-intensive goods and services has fallen this year, so he saw little need for higher interest rates. Others were more cautious. An analyst at J.P. Morgan Personal Investing said firms report renewed cost pressures, although wage growth in the private sector is muted and the labour market is soft.

Rising costs could also hurt spending. A consultant warned that households facing back-to-school costs and possibly higher interest rates might spend less in the final quarter of the year, squeezing retailers' margins. Markets expected the Bank of England to hold rates at 3.75% but anticipated a rise in November.

Inflation reduces the purchasing power of incomes and affects decisions by households, firms and the Bank of England. This article shows how a supply-side shock from abroad can raise the price level, and why policymakers must judge whether it will pass into wider prices and wages before they respond.

concepts: Cost-push inflation and a shift left of short-run aggregate supply
External shocks and a net importer of energy
chain: The conflict involving Iran pushes crude oil above $100 a barrel.
Fuel and household energy costs rise, raising firms' costs of production and transport.
Short-run aggregate supply shifts left and the general price level rises, taking inflation to 3.1%.
The UK imports much of its energy, so it has little control over the price.
If firms pass on costs and workers seek higher pay, inflation could spread and the Bank of England may raise interest rates.
Higher prices cut real incomes, which could weaken consumer spending and retailers' profits.

evaluation.label: Magnitude
evaluation.text: inflation is only 0.1 percentage points above 3%, and food inflation is low at 1.1%, so the shock may be limited.

evaluation.label: Duration
evaluation.text: the effects depend on how long the conflict and high oil prices last.

evaluation.label: Wage pressure
evaluation.text: the article says private sector wage growth is muted and the labour market is soft, which reduces the risk of a wage-price spiral.

key_terms.definition: A sustained increase in the general price level, usually measured as an annual percentage change.
The main measure of UK inflation, which tracks the cost of a typical basket of goods and services bought by households.
A rise in the general price level caused by higher costs of production.
A country that buys more of a good from abroad than it sells abroad.
A limit set by the regulator on the price that energy suppliers can charge households.
The return on UK government bonds, which reflects the cost of government borrowing.
Further price rises that occur when firms and workers respond to an initial price rise, for example through higher wages.
Income adjusted for inflation, which shows what it can actually buy.

questions.prompt: An item cost £50 in August last year. If its price rose by the UK's annual inflation rate of 3.1%, what would it cost now?
Which change best explains cost-push inflation caused by higher oil prices?
questions.explanation: Higher costs of production reduce the output firms will supply at each price level, shifting SRAS left and raising prices.

questions.prompt: Why is the UK described as particularly vulnerable to energy price shocks?

options.text: It exports most of the energy it produces
It is a net importer of energy, so global price rises increase its costs
It has no central bank to control inflation
It uses a price cap on food

questions.explanation: As a net importer, the UK must pay higher world prices, which raises costs for firms and households.

questions.prompt: Explain how higher fuel prices can lead to cost-push inflation.

points: Identifies that fuel is a cost of production or transport for firms.
Uses the article, for example motor fuel prices 23% higher than a year earlier, crude oil above $100 a barrel or inflation at 3.1%.

Develops a chain, for example: higher fuel costs raise firms' costs of production (1), so firms pass on the cost through higher prices and short-run aggregate supply falls, raising the general price level (1).

notes: Award 1 mark for a partial chain and 2 for a complete one.

questions.prompt: Assess the likely impact of higher inflation on UK households and firms.

points: Inflation lowers the purchasing power of money and real incomes.
Firms face higher costs and may cut spending.
Interest rates may rise in response.
Motor fuel up 23% and household fuels up 6% year on year.
Household budgets squeezed by back-to-school costs.
Markets expecting a rate rise in November.
For households: higher prices reduce real incomes and consumption, and higher mortgage rates could add to the squeeze.
For firms: higher energy and input costs reduce profit margins unless costs are passed on, and weaker consumer spending reduces revenue for retailers.

Judge using the size of the rise (a small change to 3.1%), the fact that food inflation is only 1.1%, muted wage growth, the duration of the energy shock, and the difference between groups such as low-income households, who spend more of their income on fuel, and firms that can pass on costs.
A supported conclusion should say who is most affected and why.

discussion.prompt: Is a rise in inflation from 2.9% to 3.1% a real problem for households, or is it too small to worry about?

points.label: ING
points.text: There is very little sign that the energy shock is spreading to other prices. Food inflation slipped to 1.1%, so there is no strong case for higher interest rates.

points.label: J.P. Morgan Personal Investing
points.text: The rise is unlikely to make the Bank raise rates yet, but firms report renewed cost pressures. Private sector pay growth is muted and the labour market is soft.

points.label: McKinsey & Company
points.text: The highest fuel prices in nearly four years could make the retailers' key 'golden quarter' uncertain, with households facing back-to-school costs and possibly higher interest rates.
